receipts.label: Del Mar Station Transit Village (Pasadena) — Metro joint development on public land
receipts.source_title: Del Mar Station — Congress for the New Urbanism
receipts.extract: Del Mar Station Transit Village, Pasadena: 3.4-acre site owned by LA Metro (property returned to public hands when Amtrak service ended 1994); 347 residential units with 15% affordable; 1,200-space subterranean garage of which 600 spaces reserved for commuters; 20,000 sf retail; restored 1925 Santa Fe depot. Gold Line Del Mar station opened 2003. CNU Charter Award 2003.
receipts.notes: The 2003-line Pasadena comparable: public land, joint development, mixed use, celebrated as model TOD.

receipts.label: Urban Partners selection by MTA and mid-construction sale to Archstone REIT
receipts.source_title: Light Rail Trains Carry Development in Pasadena
receipts.extract: Urban Partners was selected by the L.A. County Metropolitan Transportation Authority in 2000 from among 11 bidders to develop the Del Mar site. Urban Partners sold the development in December 2004, mid-construction, to Archstone, a Denver-based real estate investment trust.
receipts.notes: Extract via search result summary of LABJ coverage; documents competitive public selection and institutional-capital exit as normal course.

receipts.label: BID prevalence in the United States
receipts.source_title: Business improvement districts in the United States
receipts.extract: Per the 2011 International Downtown Association census there were 1,002 BIDs in the United States; by 2010 they had been implemented in nearly 1,000 major cities and small towns, with New York City alone containing 78 districts. California BID types: property-based, business-based, and tourism-based. Cites the Property and Business Improvement District Law of 1994 (initial 5-year term, 10-year renewals) and the Parking and Business Improvement Area Law of 1989.
receipts.notes: Tertiary source; used only for order-of-magnitude prevalence and enabling-law identification.

receipts.label: Property and Business Improvement District Law of 1994 (enabling statute)
receipts.source_title: Streets and Highways Code, Division 18, Part 7 — Property and Business Improvement District Law of 1994
receipts.extract: The Property and Business Improvement District Law of 1994 is codified at California Streets and Highways Code sections 36600 et seq.; districts formed under it may be funded by assessments against businesses, assessments against real property, or a combination.
receipts.notes: Statute existence and citation confirmed via legislature site and Justia code listing in search results; general-law authority available to every California city.

receipts.label: Old Pasadena Management District / Pasadena PBIDs
receipts.source_title: Old Pasadena Management District
receipts.extract: The Old Pasadena Management District contracts with the City of Pasadena to manage the Old Pasadena Business Improvement District, formed in 2000; it funds district-wide security, marketing, and maintenance financed through annual assessments on privately owned commercial property. The City of Pasadena maintains multiple Property-Based Improvement Districts (per cityofpasadena.net PBID page).
receipts.notes: Direct fetch returned 403; extract assembled from search-result snippets of oldpasadena.org and cityofpasadena.net pages. Shows BID governance standard in the corridor's flagship downtown, adjacent to 2003 Gold Line stations.

receipts.label: LA Metro Joint Development Program
receipts.source_title: Joint Development — LA Metro
receipts.publisher: Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority
receipts.extract: Metro's Joint Development is 'the real estate development program through which Metro collaborates with developers to deliver transit-oriented developments on Metro-owned properties.' Metro seeks to grow its portfolio to 10,000 homes by 2031, half income-restricted, and has identified roughly 200 development opportunities ('10K Sites') to be offered through competitive developer proposals. Joint Development Strategic Plan (December 2023) and updated Policy (July 2025) referenced.
receipts.notes: Public agency itself institutionalizes station-adjacent private development — the sequence is policy, not anomaly.

receipts.label: SB 375 (Sustainable Communities and Climate Protection Act of 2008)
receipts.source_title: Sustainable Communities and Climate Protection Act of 2008
receipts.extract: SB 375, signed September 30, 2008, requires CARB to set regional per-capita GHG reduction targets and each MPO to adopt a Sustainable Communities Strategy integrating transportation, land use, and housing; it streamlines CEQA review for projects consistent with the regional strategy, particularly transit-oriented and infill development.
receipts.notes: State-level policy driver making station-area densification the mandated regional planning default across California since 2008.

receipts.label: Brooks & Lutz — urban land assembly premium (peer-reviewed, LA data)
receipts.source_title: From Today's City to Tomorrow's City: An Empirical Investigation of Urban Land Assembly (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 2016, 8(3):69-105, doi:10.1257/pol.20130399)
receipts.extract: 'We hypothesize that in the absence of market frictions such as holdouts, the price of land sold for assembly should not exceed the price of land sold for other uses. Empirically, we find that to-be-assembled land in Los Angeles trades at a 15 to 40 percent premium and conclude that significant frictions prevent assembly.' Built from Los Angeles County Assessor parcel data.
receipts.notes: PDF retrieved and text extracted directly. Core counterfactual input: without an assembler willing to pay the premium, fragmented parcel fabric persists.

receipts.label: Fejarang 1993 — LA Metro Rail announcement effects on property values
receipts.source_title: Impact on Property Values: A Study of the Los Angeles Metro Rail (Fejarang, R.A., 1993)
receipts.extract: Study of whether the 1983-1988 announcement/actualization of Los Angeles Metro Rail funding affected residential property values pre-opening, covering 1980-1990 with a pre-test/post-test control-group design: 'property values after the period of actualisation were found to be significantly different from property values before the period of actualisation,' with properties near planned stations valued measurably differently from those farther away.
receipts.notes: Documents anticipation-phase capitalization near planned LA stations as a market-wide phenomenon dating to the system's origin — buying after announcement, before opening, is ordinary de-risked investment behavior.

receipts.label: Miceli & Sirmans — holdout problem, urban sprawl, and eminent domain
receipts.source_title: The holdout problem, urban sprawl, and eminent domain (Journal of Housing Economics, 2007)
receipts.extract: Developers attempting land assembly face a potential holdout problem that raises the cost of development; to minimize this cost developers prefer land whose ownership is less dispersed, creating a bias toward development at the urban fringe where average lot sizes are larger, resulting in urban sprawl.
receipts.notes: Abstract-level content obtained via search results; full text paywalled. Complements cf-r17: fragmented small-lot downtown ownership systematically deters redevelopment absent assembly.

receipts.label: Crenshaw/LAX (K Line) corridor speculation and development reporting
receipts.source_title: Crenshaw/LAX rail line draws development to South LA
receipts.extract: Speculative investors described as 'scrambling to get prime land along the rail line,' much of it favorably zoned for commercial or high-density housing. Business owner Victoria Fortson: 'The building beside me is now $2.5 million; a couple of years ago it was $535,000.' About 5,000 residential units planned or under construction between the Expo Line station in West Adams and Hyde Park (CBRE). New York investors bought Baldwin Hills Crenshaw Plaza for $141M; Harridge Development plans $1B mixed-use redevelopment of the 42-acre site. The $2.1B line opened partially October 2022.
receipts.notes: Same shape on a different corridor: public rail investment, favorable zoning, land acquisition around opening, institutional developer, sharp land-value uplift.

inputs.label: Baldwin buys Rancho Santa Anita for $200,000

claims.plain: Lucky Baldwin bought Rancho Santa Anita (~8,000-8,500 acres) from Harris Newmark in 1875 for $200,000, then a record price for greater Los Angeles property.

receipts.label: Rancho Santa Anita ownership chain
receipts.source_title: Rancho Santa Anita
receipts.extract: 13,319-acre grant to Hugo Reid (adobe built 1839; formal recognition 1845). Reid sold to Henry Dalton 1847 for $2,700; US patent to Dalton 1866. Joseph Rowe purchased 1854 ($33,000); Albert Dibblee and William Corbett 1858-1864; William Wolfskill bought 11,319 acres 1865 ($20,000); Luis Wolfskill sold 8,500 acres with the lake to Harris Newmark ($85,000); Newmark sold to E.J. 'Lucky' Baldwin in 1875 for $200,000. Baldwin founded a racetrack (opened 1907 era; closed 1909, burned 1912); Santa Anita Park opened 1934.
receipts.notes: Tertiary source; grant chain corroborated in outline by Homestead Museum blog (lh-r19) and Arboretum-derived sources. Grant year given variously as 1841 (initial) and 1845 (full grant).

receipts.label: Wikipedia: Arcadia, California
receipts.source_title: Arcadia, California
receipts.extract: Arcadia incorporated August 5, 1903; Lucky Baldwin was its first mayor, having purchased 8,000 acres of Rancho Santa Anita in 1875. City lies in the San Gabriel Valley at the base of the San Gabriel Mountains, about 13 miles NE of downtown LA. In 1885 the Los Angeles and San Gabriel Valley Railroad, in which Baldwin held stock, opened a line through the ranch, enabling subdivision; the line later became part of the Santa Fe network. Population grew from 9,122 (1940) to 23,066 (1950); 56,681 by 2020.
receipts.notes: Incorporation date and mayor role corroborated by LAist (lh-r10).

receipts.label: Homestead Museum blog: Rancho Santa Anita 1870s
receipts.source_title: La La Landscapes: Rancho Santa Anita, late 1870s
receipts.publisher: Workman and Temple Family Homestead Museum
receipts.extract: The ranch sat just below the Sierra Madre (later San Gabriel) Mountains, 'endowed with plenty of water from creeks and springs' and a stunning natural lake. Harris Newmark, who had purchased the ranch in 1872 for $85,000, sold it to Baldwin for $200,000 — described as the highest price yet paid for any property in greater Los Angeles at that time. Over 34 years Baldwin developed the estate (Queen Anne cottage by the lake, thoroughbreds) and facilitated establishment of the town of Arcadia during the 1880s boom.
receipts.notes: Museum-authored history; documents the ranch's spring/creek water endowment under Baldwin.

receipts.source_title: Alyeupkigna, California
receipts.extract: Alyeupkigna was a Tongva-Gabrieleno settlement in the San Gabriel Valley at Santa Anita, at the base of Little Santa Anita Canyon; site now within the Los Angeles County Arboretum and the city of Arcadia (approx. 34.14556 N, 118.04972 W). receipts.extract: Arcadia incorporated August 5, 1903; Lucky Baldwin was its first mayor, having purchased 8,000 acres of Rancho Santa Anita in 1875. City lies in the San Gabriel Valley at the base of the San Gabriel Mountains, about 13 miles NE of downtown LA. receipts.label: LAist/KPCC on Baldwin's Arcadia
receipts.source_title: Lucky Baldwin's Arcadia: A 'gambling hell and booze pleasure park'
receipts.extract: Arcadia incorporated in 1903 with Lucky Baldwin as its first mayor, despite promising county supervisors he would not establish a town for 'horse racing, gambling, and other kindred vices.' One of Arcadia's first ordinances licensed alcohol sales; Baldwin's eldest daughter received the first liquor license. His 1907 track featured slot machines, roulette, poker rooms, bars serving his wines and brandies. Opponents feared a 'gambling hell and booze pleasure park'; incorporation election rolls were about 75 percent Baldwin relatives, associates, or employees. Baldwin died 1909; liquor licensing outlawed by 1912.
receipts.notes: Journalistic history segment (Off-Ramp).

receipts.label: L.A. TACO Arcadia history feature
receipts.source_title: Arcadia: 11 Things About The Neighborhood's History You May Not Know
receipts.extract: Arcadia established where the Tongva settlement 'Aleupkinga' stood; Spanish colonization and the mission system brought forced removal and land seizure. Arcadia incorporated 1903 with about 500 residents, its economy 'largely based on entertainment, sporting, hospitality, and gambling,' much of it Baldwin's ventures. Baldwin's racetrack fizzled in 1909 after the state outlawed gambling. In 1942 the racetrack grounds became the 'longest running and largest processing and holding center for Americans of Japanese heritage,' detaining more than 18,000 people, including in horse stalls.
receipts.notes: Journalistic local-history listicle; used for corroboration only.

inputs.label: Baldwin's original racetrack opens (site of today's golf course)

claims.plain: Baldwin's original Santa Anita racetrack opened December 7, 1907 on the site of today's Santa Anita Golf Course / Arcadia County Park area — not the site of the present Santa Anita Park.

receipts.label: PCAD: Santa Anita Race Track #1
receipts.source_title: Santa Anita Race Track #1, Arcadia, CA
receipts.publisher: Pacific Coast Architecture Database, University of Washington Libraries
receipts.extract: The track opened December 7, 1907, organized by Elias Jackson 'Lucky' Baldwin on his Arcadia estate, with a large grandstand and paddock. It operated for only two years, closing in 1909 after the Walker-Otis Bill prohibited 'pool selling, bookmaking, or gambling on horse races in the state.' Its popularity eventually led to construction of a second Santa Anita track elsewhere on Baldwin's estate in 1933-1934. The original track has been demolished.
receipts.notes: Academic architecture database; anchors the exact Dec 7, 1907 opening date and the two-track distinction.

receipts.label: Arcadia Historical Society marker: Baldwin's 1907 racetrack
receipts.source_title: Arcadia Historical Marker 3 (Lucky Baldwin's racetrack)
receipts.extract: Baldwin's track opened in December 1907 on more than 150 acres of his ranch land near his home, on the site of today's Santa Anita Golf Course. 'The State banned horse racing in 1909, and the track was forced to close.' Baldwin died of pneumonia that same year. 'The track's grandstand burned in 1912.' Site later used as a military balloon training facility.
receipts.notes: Local historical society marker text; corroborates PCAD (lh-r13) on dates and Golf Course/Arcadia County Park location.

receipts.label: California State Library on Dec 25 1934 opening
receipts.source_title: December 25, 1934: Opening Day at Santa Anita - Celebrate California
receipts.extract: Santa Anita opened Christmas Day 1934; Los Angeles Turf Club formed by merging Northern and Southern California investor groups; Hal Roach a principal investor, Bing Crosby a shareholder; nearly 30,800 attended opening day (LA Times Dec 26). Baldwin had built an earlier racetrack adjacent to the current site (dated here 1904), which closed in 1909 (year of Baldwin's death) and burned in 1912. Reopening followed voter approval of Proposition 5 in 1933 legalizing pari-mutuel wagering. 1935 Santa Anita Handicap offered a $100,000 purse.
receipts.notes: State library educational feature. Its '1904' refers to track organization/construction; opening was Dec 7, 1907 per PCAD (lh-r13).

receipts.source_title: Arcadia Historical Marker 6 (Santa Anita Park)

receipts.label: Wikipedia: Santa Anita Park
receipts.source_title: Santa Anita Park
receipts.extract: Opened Christmas Day 1934; investor groups led by Dr. Charles H. 'Doc' Strub (San Francisco) and producer Hal Roach (Los Angeles) merged to form the Los Angeles Turf Club. Architect Gordon Kaufmann designed buildings in Colonial Revival and Streamline Moderne styles (Persian Green and Chiffon Yellow). Baldwin built a racetrack adjacent to the present site (organized 1904); it closed after the 1909 Walker-Otis anti-gambling law and burned in 1912. Meditrust acquired Santa Anita Companies 1997; Magna Entertainment Corp. then purchased the track; Stronach Group owner 2011-present. 1942 Santa Anita Assembly Center held over 18,000 people; racing resumed 1945.
receipts.notes: Consistent with markers (lh-r05), State Library (lh-r06), and Stronach Group page (lh-r11).

claims.plain: The Raymond Basin was adjudicated in City of Pasadena v. City of Alhambra (filed 1937; judgment December 23, 1944; affirmed 1949) — the first groundwater adjudication in California — with the Raymond Basin Management Board as watermaster and Arcadia among party agencies.

receipts.label: DWR Bulletin 118 Raymond Groundwater Basin (4-23)
receipts.source_title: California's Groundwater Bulletin 118 - Raymond Groundwater Basin (last update 2/27/04)
receipts.extract: Raymond Basin: 26,200 acres, NW San Gabriel Valley; SE boundary is the Raymond fault. Water-bearing materials are Quaternary alluvial gravel/sand/silt deposited by streams flowing out of the San Gabriel Mountains. 'The Raymond fault... acts as a groundwater barrier along the southern boundary... a complete barrier along its western end... East of Santa Anita Wash, this fault ceases to be an effective barrier.' Principal recharge streams: Arroyo Seco, Eaton Creek, Santa Anita Creek. 'The Raymond Basin was adjudicated in 1944'; watermaster is Raymond Basin Management Board; City of Arcadia listed among water agencies.
receipts.notes: PDF retrieved and read in full (5 pages).

receipts.label: Arroyo Seco Foundation: Raymond Basin adjudication history
receipts.source_title: History of the Raymond Basin Adjudication
receipts.extract: Pasadena sued Alhambra and other major water users in 1937 (City of Pasadena v. City of Alhambra et al.) to adjudicate basin water rights and end annual overdraft. The Division of Water Resources determined safe yield of 21,000 acre-feet/year against withdrawals of 29,000. On December 23, 1944 Judge Frank Collier approved the stipulated judgment using 'mutual prescription' — each party's decreed right cut roughly one-third, all of equal priority. The California Supreme Court affirmed in 1949. Described as 'the first groundwater adjudication... in California and the first to use the California Division of Water Resources to determine water rights.'
receipts.notes: Nonprofit watershed organization history; 1944 adjudication independently confirmed by DWR Bulletin 118 (lh-r03).

TCR (Dallas-based multifamily arm of Crow Holdings) approved for seven-story, 319-unit complex at 150 North Santa Anita Avenue; 26 affordable units via density bonus; 570 parking spaces; designed by Studio One Eleven; retains adjacent eight-story office building and one-story bank; construction expected 26 months, completion August 2025 (estimate at time). Landowner/seller not named. Ken Valach named as TCR CEO.
receipts.notes: Corroborates ow-r07.

inputs.label: TCR / Positive Investments JV buys the 2.9-acre Alexan Azalea site (8 years after station opening)

claims.plain: In April 2024 a joint venture of Trammell Crow Residential and Positive Investments purchased the 2.9-acre site adjacent to the Arcadia station (Santa Anita Ave / Santa Clara St / Wheeler Ave) for the 319-unit Alexan Azalea project; the seller and price were not disclosed.
claims.qualification: This purchase postdates the station opening by about eight years. Deed chronology for the underlying block is now resolved: Positive Investments held the parent parcel since 2018-01-24 (see clm-pi-azalea-2018); the office tower retained its 2018 assessment while only the carved-out development parcels were reassessed at the 2024 sale, consistent with — but not proof of — a Positive-affiliated grantor. The named seller on the 2024 deed itself remains unresolved after search.

receipts.label: CBRE press release on April 2024 sale of 2.9-acre Arcadia site
receipts.source_title: CBRE Announces Sale of 2.9-Acre Development Site in Arcadia, California
receipts.extract: 'CBRE has arranged the sale of a 2.9-acre development site several parcels of land in Arcadia, Calif.' Dated April 22, 2024. Buyer: joint venture of Trammell Crow Residential (TCR) and Positive Investments. Site 'between Santa Anita Avenue, Santa Clara Street and Wheeler Avenue' adjacent to the Arcadia Gold Line station. Price not disclosed. Seller not identified.
receipts.notes: Broker's own release does not name the seller.

receipts.label: Connect CRE story on the April 2024 sale (search-snippet only; page 403s)
receipts.source_title: Trammell Crow Residential Nabs Arcadia Development Site
receipts.extract: Search-retrieved snippet: 'Dean Zander and Stewart Weston of CBRE and John Montakab of Walker & Dunlop facilitated the sale on behalf of the buyer, a joint venture between Trammell Crow Residential (TCR) and Arcadia-based Positive Investments... TCR plans a 319-unit multifamily development under its Alexan brand on the 2.2 acres of land adjacent to the existing structures.' Reported April 25, 2024.
receipts.notes: Direct fetch returned HTTP 403 (twice, incl. browser UA); web.archive.org snapshot exists but archive.org is egress-blocked. Extract is from the search-engine snippet actually returned to us. Brokers acted for the BUYER; seller unnamed.

receipts.label: CBRE press release: sale of 2.9-acre Arcadia development site to TCR/Positive Investments JV
receipts.source_title: CBRE Announces Sale of 2.9-Acre Development Site in Arcadia, California
receipts.extract: Press release dated April 22, 2024. Buyer: joint venture between Trammell Crow Residential (TCR) and Positive Investments. Site adjacent to the Arcadia Gold Line light-rail station, between Santa Anita Avenue, Santa Clara Street and Wheeler Avenue. Brokers: Dean Zander and Stewart Weston (CBRE), John Montakab (Walker & Dunlop). Planned 319-unit Alexan-branded multifamily project, seven-story podium, 575 parking spaces, outdoor plaza, pedestrian access to station. Prior improvements: parking lots, an eight-story office building and a single-story bank building. Seller not identified; price not stated.
receipts.notes: Party press release; seller and price undisclosed.

receipts.label: DAIA Facebook video featuring Erik Wahl touring Alexan Azalea
receipts.source_title: Downtown Arcadia is growing, and we got a sneak peek! Erik Wahl from Positive Inves...
receipts.extract: Video tour of the Alexan Azalea project at 34 E. Santa Clara St. in Downtown Arcadia. Erik Wahl described as President of the Downtown Arcadia Improvement Association and 'from Positive Investments.' Quote: 'This will be a 7-story mixed-use residential with 319 new apartments, including 26 affordable units, parking for 551 vehicles.' Expected opening January 2027. Post date not shown in retrieved content.
receipts.notes: DAIA self-published; establishes affiliation phrase 'from Positive Investments' but no corporate title.

claims.plain: Positive Investments, Inc. is an active California corporation (entity 1362091, registered January 8, 1986; self-claims a 1976 founding) headquartered in Arcadia, with filed officers Rao R. Yalamanchili (Director/CEO/agent), Srinivas Yalamanchili (Director/Secretary), and Vipula Yalamanchili (Director/CFO).
claims.qualification: From an aggregator of CA SOS data; the SOS portal itself was bot-blocked (unavailable after search). The 1976/1986 founding discrepancy is recorded, not resolved.

inputs.label: Arcadia Town Center five-parcel consolidation (181 units) approved

claims.plain: Arcadia Town Center, LLC (project manager Ben Zhang; consultant Psomas) obtained approval January 14, 2025 to consolidate five parcels (2.27 acres, APNs 5775-025-032/-033/-034/-037/-038) at Huntington/Santa Anita into a 181-unit mixed-use project.

receipts.label: CEQAnet record: Arcadia Town Center MND
receipts.source_title: Arcadia Town Center - CEQAnet
receipts.publisher: California Governor's Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation (CEQAnet)
receipts.extract: Arcadia Town Center, 5-19 West Huntington Drive and 25-75 North Santa Anita Avenue, Arcadia. APNs 5775-025-032, -033, -034, -037, -038. Lead agency: City of Arcadia. Applicant: Arcadia Town Center, LLC (Ben Zhang, Project Manager). Consolidates five parcels (2.27 acres): 181 residential units, 13,130 sq ft ground-floor commercial, 378 parking spaces, five stories/60 feet. MND public review 11/21/2024-12/20/2024. Consultant: Jillian Neary, Psomas. City contact: Edwin Arreola, Senior Planner.
receipts.notes: Official CEQA clearinghouse record.

receipts.label: CEQAnet Notice of Determination: Arcadia Town Center approval
receipts.source_title: Arcadia Town Center Project - NOD
receipts.extract: Notice of Determination posted 1/16/2025; project approved 1/14/2025. Mixed-use development consolidating five parcels (2.27 acres): 181 residential units, ~13,130 sq ft ground-floor commercial, 378 parking spaces (one subterranean level), five stories/60 feet. Includes upsizing ~1.3 miles of sewer line along Santa Anita Avenue. Existing site uses not specified in NOD.
receipts.notes: Approval date anchor for Arcadia Town Center.

inputs.label: First Avenue arterial pavement rehabilitation bid (Prop C/STPL exchange)

claims.plain: The current First Avenue project is 'Arterial Pavement Rehabilitation - First Avenue between Huntington Dr and Duarte Rd': grind-and-overlay plus curb and gutter, curb ramps, sidewalks, and pedestrian-safety bulb-outs, funded by Prop C via a federal STPL fund exchange with LA Metro, bid March 2026 with bids above budget.
claims.qualification: No water-main or utility scope appears in the CIP sheet; a separately named 'First Avenue Corridor Improvements' CIP project exists with no published scope (unavailable after search).
